l\.s we approach the 146th Convention in Chicago, we must ad
dress the most critical issue facing fraternities on a national level
today �
how to emphasize and continue to make available the
positive aspects of a fraternity experience and likewise how to elim
inate the negative aspects involved in hazing, substance abuse, and
sexual abuse.
We are facing a relatively unsettled period in the history of
fraternities. In spite of the fact that there are more fraternity chap
ters than ever before, more fraternity members than ever before,
and more campuses with fraternity systems than ever before, our
existence is constantly called into question because of recurring
incidents involving substance abuse, sexual abuse, and hazing or a
combination of these elements. Newspapers, television and other
media are filled with negative articles about incidents involving
fraternities; colleges and universities around the country are taking
"hard looks" at their fraternity and sorority systems, including Bowdoin and Wesleyan, to name only two where Psi Upsilon has chap
ters. Other colleges and universities are utilizing the "unrest" about
fraternities to limit rushing opportunities, including Dartmouth and
Northwestern. In short, in spite of the positive efforts made by
national fraternities and their chapters to continue to provide the
opportunity for undergraduates to build leadership and interper
sonal skills that are not often found on campuses today, fraternities
are being justifiably attacked frontally on a continuing and unre
lenting basis!
This environment has resulted in a very serious self-study by our
interfraternity leadership. Beginning in September, 1988, at a spe
cial meeting of the Fraternity Executives Association (FEA), the
full-time professional executives of our national and international
fraternities carefully reviewed the existing fraternity environment
and concluded that, in spite of enormous efforts over the last decade
or more, hazing (and the associated alcohol abuse and sometimes
sexual abuse) has not been eradicated and continues to provide the
greatest cause for concern in the fraternity world. Further, the
FEA concluded that the basic cause of these problems is a structural
problem that fraternities have created in the form of "pledgeship,
"
which provides the opportunity for hazing and its associated prob
lems to occur. As a result, the FEA voted to seek the abolition of
pledgeship as a
part of the fraternity experience in order to fully
eradicate the opportunities for these negative elements.
Just before the FEA took this action, Zeta Beta Tau Fraternity
voted to eliminate pledging and introduce a variety of alternatives
for fraternity education, each based on the premise offull admission
to membership prior to such education. Subsequently, Tau Kappa
Epsilon completed a major study of alternatives to pledging and
Lambda Chi Alpha began exploring further refinements to their
already existing "Associate Member" program. In addition. Kappa
Delta Rho has also voted to eliminate pledging.
At the NIC Annual Meeting in December, 1988, the national
and international fraternity presidents discussed the FEA resolu
tion at length and, as a result, several resolutions on the topic were
introduced to the NIC delegates. The NIC delegates ultimately
adopted a resolution asking member fraternities to study alterna
tives to pledging and report back to the NIC at their Annual Meet
ing this December.
Our own Executive Council first took up the pledging issue at
our October, 1988, Executive Council meeting in New York fol
lowing a
report by Executive Director Kathy McGlone on the FEA
resolution. Further discussions were held at the December and
April Executive Council meetings. This issue also consumed a sig
nificant amount of time at the Undergraduate Advisory Board meet
ing held in Paoli in June, 1989. As a result of these deliberations,
the Executive Committee voted at its June, 1989 meeting to es
tablish a Task Force on Brotherhood. This Task Force, chaired by
Mark D. Bauer, Omega' 83, and consisting of the Chairman and
Vice Chairman of the Undergraduate Advisory Board, Jeffrey D.
Hurwitz, Xi '90, and Joel VV. Anderson, Epsilon Nu '91, and Ex
ecutive Council member Richard D. Dadey, Pi '80, and Brother
Mark A. Williams, Phi "76, has as its initial charge to provide a
background report on the subject of alternatives to pledging to the
Executive Council and the upcoming 146th Convention. The Task
Force will be surveying undergraduate brothers initially in prep
aration for this report. I anticipate that, in addition, the Task Force
will also complete the work of the Task Force on Ritual, which was
established several years ago to add to our existing rituals.
This issue is a serious and complicated one that must command
our full attention. No one can approach the issue of doing away
with pledgeship without serious trepidation. It appears that, unless
we can find ways that are more successful than those of the recent
past to eliminate these "hazards to our health," we may be faced
with no alternative but to completely eliminate pledgeship as the
environment in which these evils thrive. I urge each of you to
seriously consider how we can collectively and constructively ad
dress this problem. Send your thoughts to the Task Force at the
International Office �
the sooner the better!
And . . . come to the 146th Convention in Chicago from August
17th to the 20th, hear the results of the Task Force's work, and
take part in the resolution of this important issue.
Yours in the bonds.
William R. Robie, Epsilon Omega '66

a student's academic performance. That
is the major finding of a study released
by the Washington Higher Education
Coordination Board in Olympia. The
study, conducted by Augenblick, 'Van de
Water & Associates of Denver, Colorado,
examined student records and student
survey responses for 3,608 students re
ceiving financial aid and enrolled in twelve
public and private colleges.
For the population studied, students
who work tend to do slightly better ac
ademically than students who do not
work. Working students do, however,
tend to take slightly longer to finish a
degree program

completion rates than students who do
not work.

hours per week (up to 20 hours).
� Students who are financiall independ
ent of their parents do better academ
ically than students who are financially
dependent on their parents.

SPEAKING OF THE FOUNDATION
The First Thirty Years (Continued)
An innovation in the last issue of "The Diamond" was the first in a
series of columns describing the Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. and the
increasingly significant role it is destined to serve in the future of our
fraternity.
That initial column recounted the Foundation's establishment in 1958
as an educational and philanthropic corporation, primarily to provide
financial assistance to needy and deserving students. Beyond this, at
the same time, it was broadly designed to encourage and promote schol
arship, character, and morality.
An impressive mailing went out to our 17,000 living alumni of that
day, announcing this new 501(c)(3) organization and appealing for tax
deductible contributions.
Funds came in slowly. For the most part they constituted bequests
from devoted alumni imbued with the Psi Upsilon spirit of the helping
hand.
Twenty-three years went by, and a modest corpus of about $250,000
had been accumulated.
A partial fulfillment of the Foundation's first stipulated purpose was
implemented just a year after its founding with one $30 scholarship
awarded to an undergraduate of the Psi Chapter.
Two grants of $100 each followed the next year. By 1981, the schol
arship program had grown to 23 awards annually, averaging $485 and
totaling $11,150. This constituted the Foundation's principal thrust in
those early years and remains so today.
The year 1981 was a year of reckoning. Two factors had become
increasingly clear: (1) the cost of Fraternity services was increasing at a
faster rate than Fraternity income, despite the continuing and com
mendable growth of the Annual Giving program, which accounted for
over one-half of the Fraternity's revenues; and (2) new needs were
developing for the oncoming generations of undergraduates that Psi
Upsilon was uniquely equipped and positioned to meet, if funds could
be found.
And so was born the Sesquicentennial Fund, a capital fund-raising
program named for the 150th anniversary of the founding of Psi Upsilon
in 1833. The Foundation's Board of Directors and the Fraternity's Ex
ecutive Council joined forces in shaping and backing the most ambitious
effort ever undertaken by the Garnet and Gold.
Close at hand now was the realization of the prediction envisioned in
the original prospectus for the Foundation, inviting all living members
of the Fraternity "to join in a program that well may become the most
noteworthy of the fine projects with which the name of Psi Upsilon has
been associated throughout its illustrious history."
Our next installment will focus on the decade of the '80's.
Henry B .

Kaiser Steps Down
Robert L. Kaiser
Zeta '39
Robert L. Kaiser, Zeta '39, has re
cently stepped down as president of The
Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc., a position
which he has filled with distinction since
April, 1985. Succeeding Bob is Carl A.
Beck, Delta '41.
Brother Kaiser has been a director of the foundation since 1983 and a member
of the Executive Council since 1978, serving as vice president of the Executive
Council from 1982 to 1987. His commitment to Psi U is further demonstrated
by his devotion and loyalty to the Zeta Chapter. As faculty advisor to the Chapter
and member of the alumni association since 1965, Brother Kaiser (as well as his
wife Evelyn, Zeta '83H) has provided unparalleled guidance and assistance to
both undergraduates and alumni.
Brother Kaiser graduated Phi Beta Kappa fi-om Dartmouth College with a
degree in Economics. Following graduation, he joined the N. W. Ayer Adver
tising Agency, where he worked for two years, until his enlistment in the Army.
While in the service, he attended field artillery Officer Candidate School and
served with Patton's Third Army as a
gunnery expert. He was discharged in
1945 (with two bronze stars) but continued to serve in the active reserve until
1962, retiring as a lieutenant colonel. After World War II Brother Kaiser became
chief executive officer of three industrial subsidiaries of Magnus Chemical Com
pany in New Jersey. Magnus Chemical was bought out in 1964, and Bob went
on to work for Dartmouth.
His involvement in Dartmouth's development activities began in 1965, when
he arrived as associate director of the Bequests and Estate Planning Program.
For the next eight years he administered the program without assistance and,
from 1979 to 1984, he served as co-director of Bequest and Estate Planning. In
1984, Brother Kaiser elected to become a full-time senior advisor, shifting from
an administrative role to an
advisory one. Brother Kaiser developed Dartmouth's
Bequest and Estate Planning Program into one of the most successful giving
programs in the country. Long considered the tax expert at Dartmouth, Bob is
often called upon by alumni, colleagues, and faculty members for advice.
More recently, in the past year Brother Kaiser has received both the Glass
of '39's "Man of the Year" award and Dartmouth's Alumni Award "for the many
years of contributing to Dartmouth through volunteer service to his class and
fraternity, and for his educational fundraising and creation of a
Bequest and
Trust program that has become a model for other schools." In addition, the
reconstructed basement recreation room of the Zeta Chapter house has loeen
permanently dedicated to Bob, named appropriately, the "Kaiser Room."
The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. has come a long way under the leadership
of Bob Kaiser. He will now serve as an
Honorary Life Member of the Foundation,
turning the reigns over to the more than capable hands of Carl Beck. The next
issue of The Diamond will take a closer look at the Foundation's new President,
as Brother Beck leads the Foundation into the nineties.

likely to recommend closing the chapters in
stead of trying to figure out some way to shape
them up.
My own institution, Colby College, ban
ished its fraternities in 1984. It was the first
college to take such a step since Williams abol
ished its fraternities more than 20 years be
fore. Amherst was next, and many other in
stitutions now seem to be preparing to follow
suit.
"Fraternities have been slow to

what they aU do say

they obviously

recognized campus organizations."
Not long after our decision at Colby, 1 gave
a talk at another college entitled "Fraternities
Are Dinosaurs." The young men in the au
dience, most of whom were wearing Greekletter T-shirts, did not appear to be amused
by the title or, for that matter, by what 1 had
to say. I liked the metaphor, hovvever; in fact,
I still do.
The heyday offraternities �
their Mesozoic
Era, so to speak �
ended in the mid 1960s.
Ever since, the fraternities have been en
gaged, like the brontosaurus, in a futile strug
gle against a
changed chmate. At the time of
the Vietnam War, fraternities began to be
viewed as altogether too "establishment," and
the number ofyoung men interested in joining
declined for years Aerward.
Today, proponents of the Greek system are
quick to point to an upturn in membership
nationvwde as evidence of recovery. Maybe
so, but more is not always better. The selec
tivity that has evoked criticism of fraternities
since their beginning is also the glue that bonds
the brothers together. When pledging is re
duced to little more than a search for warm
bodies, the bond is loosened. Alumni often
lose interest when they discover that current
members are a new breed, totally unlike
themselves, and general supervision of the
chapters is left in the hands of increasingly
unenthusiastic administrators.
As luck would have it, the time of lowest
membership coincided with the time when
inflation in this country was at its worst. Fewer
members provided fewer dollars to pay bigger
bills. Some colleges tried to help out �
after
all, it is cheaper to prop up a fraternity house
than to build a new dormitory �
but few in
stitutions were really comfortable with the ideal
of using tuition money to support a system not
equally accessible to all students. In any case
chapters had to increase the fees for mem
bership, providing a further deterrent to
pledging.
Fraternities have been slow to abandon ra
cial and religious discrimination, and the ones
on coeducational campuses have lagged be
hind even the Rotary Club in changing poli
cies of sex discrimination. That alone makes
the presence of fraternities on a campus an
embarrassment. If colleges say they do not
discriminate �
and that is exactly what they
all do say

they obviously cannot justify dis
criminatory actions by recognized campus or
ganizations.
Then there is a matter of behavior. Al
though outrageous pranks and general non
sense cannot be laid exclusively at the doors
of fraternities, it is certainly fair to say that
fraternities often exceed the norm in disrup
tive conduct �
in particular, hazing, harass
ment of women, destruction of property, and
alcohol abuse.
While fraternities on some campuses are
still in good health, many are already coma
tose. At some colleges they are little more than
horribly maintained tenements where some
men choose to live insulated from the kinds
of regulation and authority that govern con
duct in college dormitories.
Frequently now, another committee is
formed somewhere to deal with the dying
Greek system. It is a difficult task. More often
than not, a college will have to appoint two
such groups. The first will issue recommen
dations aimed at bringing fraternities back to
life in a form tolerable by today's standards.
Then the recommendations �
albeit made in
earnest �
will turn out to be impracticable.
That will necessitate a second panel, which
will be charged with the grimmer task of per
forming the last rites.
It is one of the curiosities of American higher
education that insititutions founded on prin
ciples ofopenness and freedom ever embraced
the elitist idea of fraternities in the first place.
However, it is not so
puzzling that the Greek
system has endured. The simple truth is that
men who join fraternities often have a jolly
good time and become enthusiastic alumni.
Colleges have been timid about "dealing
with the fraternity problem." At the very sug
gestion, development officers cringe and deans
prepare for protests from all sides. Our ex
perience at Colby, however, would suggest
that there is no need for such paranoia.
Colby's special investigative committee was
formed with the understanding that the mem
bers would be broadly representative of the
college community, their inquiry would be
comprehensive, and judgement would be re
served until the committee had completed its
work.
Eleven of the 19 members were fraternity
or sorority members, and their decision to
withdraw recognition from the fraternities at
Colby was not reached until the final sessions,
after eight months of careful deliberation.
The operation was not entirely painless, to
be sure. Some students and alumni were an
gry, and the colleges received more than a few
strident letters of complaint, but the reper
cussions feared by many people never mater
ialized.
This fall, for the first time, no students at
Colby remember the old fraternities. The for^
mer chapter houses were converted into coeducatioucJ residences, which have turned out
to be popular with students. Applications for
admission to Colby have soared. A recent cap
ital campaign went well over the top, and an
nual giving has increased by 64 per cent in
the three years since the fraternities were
abolished.
A few disorganized underground groups do
exist, but they are trivial annoyances and serve
only to remind us of the wisdom of our de
cision to close down their predecessors. Per
haps a few people are still truly angry, but
many more now ungrudgingly admit that the
decision was sensible and correct.
After all, Greek civilizations have died be
fore, and the world seems none the worse for
it.
